Case Study · Enterprise

0→1 enterprise workflow builder

Shaped the first end-to-end version of a workflow builder for an enterprise SaaS platform, from problem framing through the first shipped release.

Shipped 6 months · 3 phases · 0 → 40 customer workflows live

Overview

Enterprise customers were stitching approvals together over email and spreadsheets because the platform had no native way to model a multi-step process. I designed the builder from a blank canvas: the data model, the authoring surface, and the first-run experience that made a blank workflow feel approachable rather than intimidating.

Impact

0 → 40

customer workflows built in the first quarter

Why it matters. Proof the builder was usable without hand-holding, not just technically shipped.

3 →1

approval tools consolidated into one surface

Why it matters. Fewer places for a process to silently break.

62%

of pilot customers finished onboarding unassisted

Why it matters. The guided first-run replaced a support-led setup call.

0

data-model rewrites needed post-launch

Why it matters. The schema was built to hold features that weren't scoped yet.

Context

Role

Product designer, end-to-end

Timeline

6 months · 3 phases

Team

Design (me), 1 PM, 4 eng

Scope

Data model, authoring UI, first-run flow

Platform

Web · enterprise admin

Contribution

Research, IA, prototyping, UI, launch

FigmaFigJamMixpanel

The Problem

01

No native way to model a process

Customers stitched multi-step approvals together over email and spreadsheets, with no system of record.

02

A blank canvas is a blank page problem

Early prototypes that opened straight into an empty builder saw the majority of trial users abandon before finishing a single step.

03

Every customer's process was shaped differently

The data model had to hold branching, conditional, and parallel steps without becoming unreadable to build.

My Role

I owned this end to end - running the discovery interviews, defining the underlying step/condition data model with engineering, and designing both the authoring surface and the guided first-run that replaced a support-led onboarding call.

Approach

01

Understand

Interviewed 12 customers stitching approvals together manually to find the shared shape underneath their different processes.

02

Define

Settled on a step/condition primitive general enough to model every interviewed workflow without a custom exception.

03

Explore

Prototyped a blank canvas vs. a templated starting point - templates won decisively on completion rate.

04

Design

Authoring surface, step configuration panels, and the guided first-run, all sharing one visual grammar.

05

Ship

Phased rollout to a design-partner cohort before general availability.

06

Scale

Left the step/condition schema open for step types that weren't in scope for v1.

Outcome

Business Impact

Became a named reason cited in two enterprise renewals during the following quarter.

Product Impact

Validated the step/condition model as the pattern later builder features would extend rather than replace.

User Impact

Admins went from an email-and-spreadsheet process to a single system of record for approvals.

Reflection

Templates, not a blank canvas, were the actual unlock - the data model mattered less to first-time success than having something to react to and edit rather than something to originate from nothing.

Case Study · Product-Led Growth

Scaling a product-led onboarding flow

Redesigned self-serve onboarding to reduce time-to-value, working closely with growth and lifecycle marketing.

Shipped 4 months · 2 phases · time-to-value cut significantly

Overview

Self-serve signups were dropping off before ever reaching the product's core value moment. I redesigned onboarding around a single guided path to that moment, deferring every non-essential setup step to later in the lifecycle instead of front-loading them all at signup.

Impact

-38%

drop-off between signup and first core action

Why it matters. The single biggest lever available for activation, by a wide margin.

2.1x

week-1 retention for the redesigned cohort

Why it matters. Confirmed the effect held past day one, not just at signup.

5 → 1

required setup steps before first value

Why it matters. Every deferred step still got completed - just later, in context.

+19%

self-serve to paid conversion over the quarter

Why it matters. The metric growth actually cared about, not a vanity activation number.

Context

Role

Product designer

Timeline

4 months · 2 phases

Team

Design (me), growth PM, 2 eng, lifecycle marketing

Scope

Signup flow, first-run checklist, lifecycle emails

Platform

Web · self-serve product

Contribution

Flow design, experiment design, UI, copy

FigmaAmplitudeBraze

The Problem

01

Setup front-loaded before any value was shown

Five required fields stood between signup and the product's core action, and most trial users never got past them.

02

One flow served every use case equally badly

A solo user and an enterprise evaluator saw the identical checklist, tuned for neither.

03

Lifecycle email and in-product state disagreed

Emails nudged toward steps the product itself had already marked complete, undermining trust in both.

My Role

I redesigned the flow end to end alongside a growth PM - reordering which steps were required at signup versus deferred, and rebuilding the first-run checklist and its lifecycle-email counterpart to read from the same underlying state.

Approach

01

Understand

Funnel analysis pinpointed the exact step where the majority of drop-off concentrated.

02

Define

Reframed the goal from 'complete setup' to 'reach the core action' - setup became a means, not the metric.

03

Explore

A/B tested a five-step required flow against a one-step-to-value flow with the rest deferred.

04

Design

Rebuilt the first-run checklist and lifecycle emails to read from one shared completion state.

05

Ship

Rolled out to a percentage of new signups before a full rollout.

06

Scale

Deferred-step logic became the pattern later onboarding surfaces reused.

Outcome

Business Impact

Self-serve to paid conversion became the growth team's cited proof point for the deferred-setup pattern.

Product Impact

The single-shared-state pattern between checklist and lifecycle email got reused by two other onboarding surfaces.

User Impact

New users reached the product's core value in one step instead of five, with the rest completed later in context.

Reflection

The activation metric that mattered wasn't 'setup completed' at all - chasing that number would have optimized the wrong step. Reframing the goal around time-to-value first was the actual design decision; the UI changes followed from it.

Case Study · B2B

Simplifying a B2B admin console

Consolidated a sprawling settings and admin surface into a coherent information architecture used by thousands of enterprise admins.

Shipped 5 months · 3 phases · 40+ settings pages restructured

Overview

Three years of feature-by-feature growth had left the admin console with over 40 settings pages and no consistent structure between them. I audited the entire surface and rebuilt it around a single shared page grammar, so admins could predict where any setting lived instead of searching for it.

Impact

40+ → 6

settings pages consolidated into six modules

Why it matters. Fewer places to look changed how admins actually navigated, not just how the sidebar counted pages.

-45%

support tickets tagged 'can't find setting'

Why it matters. The single largest support-deflection outcome of the redesign.

1

page grammar shared by every module

Why it matters. Learning one module's layout now transferred to every other one.

100%

settings preserved through the migration

Why it matters. Consolidation without a single dropped capability.

Context

Role

Product designer

Timeline

5 months · 3 phases

Team

Design (me), 1 PM, 3 eng

Scope

Information architecture, page template, migration

Platform

Web · enterprise admin

Contribution

Audit, IA, page template, rollout

FigmaFigJamDovetail

The Problem

01

No consistent structure between settings pages

Forty-plus pages had each grown its own layout, so nothing an admin learned on one page transferred to the next.

02

Related settings lived in unrelated places

Two controls that affected the same downstream behavior could sit in entirely separate sections with no cross-reference.

03

Migrating without breaking anyone's saved workflow

Enterprise admins had built muscle memory and saved links around the existing structure - it couldn't just be replaced overnight.

My Role

I led the audit of all 40+ pages, designed the shared page template every module would use going forward, and planned the phased migration that moved admins over without breaking their existing bookmarks or workflows.

Approach

01

Understand

Catalogued all 40+ settings pages and interviewed admins about how they actually searched for a setting.

02

Define

Grouped the full inventory into six modules based on how admins conceptually grouped settings, not how engineering had shipped them.

03

Explore

Piloted the new page template on the highest-traffic module before committing sitewide.

04

Design

One shared template - header, tab structure, and search - applied across all six modules.

05

Ship

Phased the migration module by module with redirects preserving every existing bookmark.

06

Scale

New settings now default into the shared template instead of prompting a fresh layout decision.

Outcome

Business Impact

Support ticket volume tagged to settings discoverability dropped by nearly half within two months of full rollout.

Product Impact

The shared page template became the default for every new admin surface built afterward.

User Impact

Admins reported finding a setting on the first try instead of needing to search or ask support.

Reflection

Preserving every existing bookmark through the migration took longer than the redesign itself, but skipping it would have converted a usability win into a trust problem for the admins who'd built workflows around the old structure.

Case Study · Worker Assist · Honeywell

Building the first voice-assisted remote expert, from helmet to cloud

Field workers in oil and gas plants often work alone, without the context they need. We designed Worker Assist, a device-agnostic, voice-enabled SaaS platform. It connects desk-less workers to remote experts in real time across head-mounted tech (HMT), mobile, iPad and web.

Shipped 18 months · 4 platforms · 15+ customers

Overview

Every year, 2.3 million workers die from occupational accidents, and oil and gas is among the deadliest industries. Yet digital tools barely reach the plant floor. Field workers solve critical problems alone: gloves on, hands full, with a walkie-talkie and an expert who's hours away.

As the UX Designer, I led the end-to-end design of Worker Assist, a voice-first platform that puts a remote expert on the worker's helmet. Workers ask for help, share what they see and get guidance in real time, without putting their tools down.

The goal was simple: get expert help to any field worker, hands-free and in real time, so incidents are solved faster, with less rework and without flying experts in.

Impact

01/ 04

30%

decrease in on-site worker incidents within the plant

Why it matters. Fewer incidents in the industry with the highest fatality rate.

The headset

Hands-free, by voice.

Every control on the HMT can be triggered by voice, so the worker's hands never leave the job.

  • 30% decrease in on-site worker incidents within the plant. Fewer incidents in the industry with the highest fatality rate.
  • 20% improvement in the time needed to analyse a problem. Experts see what the worker sees, live.
  • 50% reduction in rework and travel costs. Experts no longer have to be physically on site to validate a fix.
  • 15+ customer acquisitions, including Shell and Reliance. Contributed to an eight-figure business impact.
  • Hands-free, by voice. Every control on the HMT can be triggered by voice, so the worker's hands never leave the job.

Context

Role

Sole Lead Experience Designer, end-to-end

Timeline

July 2022 – Dec 2023 · multiple MVPs shipped within 6 months

Team

Design (me), 2 PMs, 1 tech lead, 10 developers (15-member cross-functional team)

Scope

Remote collaboration, information library, Social Hub, equipment trends

Platform

Head-mounted tech (HMT), mobile, iPad, web

My Contribution

Stakeholder research, personas, journey mapping, storyboarding, wireframes, visual design, prototyping, UI dev support

Tools

FigmaFigJamMiroJira

The Problem

Every problem we found turned into an Experience Outcome (XO): a measurable target that the whole team designed toward.

How might we design a solution that delivers real-time, contextual information to isolated field workers, minimising downtime, improving safety, and enabling smarter, faster decision-making on the ground?

XO1

30%

Customer problem

Faster issue resolution

Reduction in the time taken to solve incidents, and 50% less rework.

Today, issues are solved with walkie-talkies, someone has to be on site to validate the fix, and external experts get flown in. Travel costs are significant, and time lost to these inefficient processes adds up to 30% per day.

Personas. Supervisor, Field Worker, Plant Manager, Maintenance Engineer, OEM Support Engineer.

XO2

20%

Customer problem

Smarter issue analysis

Improvement in issue analysis, with less manual work thanks to digital collaboration and tools.

It's hard to find current values, alarms, events and parameters across different systems. Control-room engineers and field engineers spend hours on it, and redundant searches and repetitive tasks add about 15% inefficiency to the workflow.

Personas. Field Worker, Maintenance Engineer, Maintenance Technician, Field Operator, Shift Supervisor.

XO3

35%

Customer problem

Information in the field

Quicker access to relevant information, lifting worker productivity by 30%.

Digital tools have barely reached field workers. Data is siloed across multiple systems and hard to access on site. Time lost to missing information in the field amounts to 20% per day.

Personas. Field Worker, Maintenance Engineer, Maintenance Technician, Field Operator, Shift Supervisor.

Hands-free by design

The constraint behind all three: field workers wear gloves and helmets and have their hands full of equipment, and they can't stop in the middle of a procedure to tap a screen. As one worker put it: "Hands-free solution to save my life, please!" Each XO had to be met without the worker ever taking their hands off the job.

Who we designed for

My Role

As the sole Lead Experience Designer on a 15-member cross-functional team, I led the end-to-end design process and helped launch multiple MVPs within 6 months. I worked closely with plant workers to uncover on-ground challenges through extensive user research. I interviewed more than 10 stakeholders, from field operators to maintenance engineers, and streamlined UX engagement practices. I supported the team in securing more than 15 customer acquisitions, which contributed to an eight-figure business impact.

Approach

  1. 01Discover

    Generative research into unmet needs, closed out with a PRFAQ.

  2. 02Define

    Experience Outcomes set who the user is, which pains matter and why.

  3. 03Explore

    Concepts designed and tested with customers, then turned into a prioritised backlog.

  4. 04Validate

    Tested with four personas, from field operator to maintenance engineer.

  5. 05Design

    Detailed designs validated one program increment ahead of development.

  6. 06Ship

    Built across HMT, mobile, iPad and web, then observed in use after deploy.

  7. 07Scale

    Tested and validated with customers until the needs were met.

Exploration

Before anything was built, three decisions shaped the product.

  1. 01

    Device-agnostic, not device-first

    Workers carry different devices depending on role and task.

    One ecosystem across HMT, mobile, iPad and web, with the same call and the same context on every screen.

  2. 02

    Voice as the primary input on the HMT

    Gloved hands full of tools can't use a touchscreen.

    Voice-enabled controls (camera off, mute, capture photo, zoom, flash, end call) that are visible on screen as spoken commands.

  3. 03

    Storyboard real field moments

    Abstract flows missed the context of the plant floor.

    Storyboards of real scenarios (a first-time procedure, a pump seal change, an expert reviewing captured images) drove field collaboration and efficiency and productivity flows.

Storyboard 01: First-time procedure

Four-panel storyboard of a new field operator preparing for his first procedure.

  1. Sebastian, a new field operator, is asked to shut down a reactor feed pump.
  2. It's his first time, so he opens the procedure video on his phone.
  3. He streams it to refresh how each step is done.
  4. Ready, he waits for the board operator's call to begin.

Storyboard 02: Pump seal change

Five-panel storyboard of a maintenance worker getting a remote expert's opinion mid-repair.

  4. With the guidance in view, Mukesh finishes the job.

Final Solution

Three surfaces work together: the worker's HMT in the field, the mobile app in their pocket, and the remote expert's web and iPad portal.

01

Hands-free on the HMT (delivers XO1)

The field worker calls a remote expert through the head-mounted device. The expert sees the live camera feed, asks for images, annotates them and sends guidance back. Every control can be triggered by voice, so the worker's hands never leave the job.

02

Mobile app: Social Hub & Information Library (delivers XO3)

When workers aren't on a call, they use the mobile app for remote collaboration, on-call support, procedure videos, PDFs and a Social Hub where field teams share knowledge about equipment and operations.

03

Remote expert portal: Web & iPad (delivers XO2)

Experts manage calls, favourites and frequent contacts on the web. On iPad they can review equipment trends alongside a live HMT stream while collaborating remotely.

What you're seeing

The same call on every device. The HMT puts the expert in the worker's view. The mobile app puts the plant's knowledge in their pocket. The portal gives the expert the data to decide quickly.

Outcome

Business Impact

More than 15 enterprise customer acquisitions, including Shell and Reliance, contributing to an eight-figure business impact.

Product Impact

Multiple MVPs launched within 6 months across four platforms. The foundation for a fluid connected-worker ecosystem.

User Impact

30% fewer on-site incidents, 20% faster problem analysis, and 50% less rework and travel cost.

Future scope. Build a fluid connected-worker ecosystem and integrate it with the safety inspection tracker application. Add instructional affordance, so users can easily correct errors, and distinct diction, so voice commands are clearly differentiated.

Reflection

  • Prioritise flexibility over simplicity.
  • Focus on end users, and the rest will follow.
  • Respect early customers' feedback.
  • Always focus on an inclusive approach.

Continuous Learning

Recognizing the need is the primary condition for design

Design begins with identifying a genuine need, not proposing a solution.

— Charles Eames

What it means

A form that ignores its purpose is decoration, not design.

How to apply it

Let the constraints of the job shape the object — don't impose a shape and hope the job fits.

About

I'm Rajat Sampathkumar, a product designer based in Bengaluru, India. I build systems, not just screens — eight-plus years in B2B SaaS and enterprise, most of it spent enhancing experiences, scaling products, 0→1 builds, and product-led growth.

I think of myself as an end-to-end designer: understanding a problem, crystallizing the insight underneath it, and developing a concept are as much part of the job as finalizing a design, prototyping it, and testing it with real people.

Then I go looking for the same clarity in a frame — landscape, architecture, street, travel. The two disciplines feed each other more than people expect: both are about deciding what belongs in the frame.
